primary_outcome_name: One-repetition maximum (1RM) in the free-weight back squat (chronic adaptation)
primary_outcome_instrument_scale: 1RM back squat, kg; progressive loading protocol (5 reps at 30%, 3 reps at 50% and 70%, 1 rep at 80%, then incremental single attempts to 1RM)
primary_timepoint: post-intervention (after the 6-week training programme), compared with pre-intervention baseline
contrast_reported_primary: CS vs TS, Group x Time (pre vs post) interaction on 1RM
population_detail: 36 resistance-trained (strength-trained) adults (15 females, 21 males; two recruitment waves Oct-Dec 2024 and Apr-Jun 2025), aged 18-35 years, >=1 year of strength training, relative back-squat 1RM >=1.00 kg/BM (females) or >=1.25 kg/BM (males), no current injury/illness, no WADA-prohibited substances, non-pregnant. Not a clinical/patient population.

published_estimate.quote: Analysis of 1RM revealed no significant time x group interaction (p = 0.352), but significant main effects of time (F(1, 34) = 80.67, p < 0.001) and sex (F(1, 33) = 95.13, p < 0.001) were observed. 1RM increased from pre- to posttest (p < 0.001), with small effect sizes (CS: g = 0.28 and TS: g = 0.23) (Figure 5). (Results, Section 3.2 Chronic Adaptations, p. 7 of 14; descriptive means in Table 2, p. 8 of 14). No between-group point estimate/CI for the difference in change is reported; only the omnibus interaction p-value and within-group Hedges' g values are given.

B_covariate_list: Sex (fixed-effect covariate in all chronic models). Baseline 1RM was additionally tested as a covariate but removed from the final 1RM model because it did not improve model fit / worsened residual diagnostics (retained only for the CMJ and v70 models). Age was never used as a model covariate anywhere in the paper -- it was used only as an eligibility criterion and a descriptive participant characteristic. This contradicts the registry's covars_published='Age,Sex'.
data_availability_statement: The dataset and analyses code are available at the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/mej4d).

registry_check.issues: The paper never labels ONE single outcome as 'the primary outcome' for the whole trial, and it explicitly has two separate domains (acute, single-session; chronic, 6-week pre/post). (1) The strongest signal of an intended primary outcome is the a-priori G*Power sample-size calculation, which was computed specifically 'for changes in one-repetition maximum (1RM)... with two groups and two time points (pre- and post-intervention)' (Section 2.1, p.2) -- i.e. 1RM, not CMJ, and this matches the chronic/post-intervention timeframe our registry's primary_time='post' points to. 1RM is also literally first-named among the chronic adaptation outcomes both in the abstract ('Chronic adaptations included one-repetition maximum (1RM), relative isometric peak force, muscle endurance, CMJ height, velocity at 70% 1RM (v70)...') and in Methods 2.4.4, and is analysed first in Results 3.2. CMJ height is listed 4th of 5 chronic outcomes and its chronic result was explicitly null ('Neither protocol improved CMJ height', Discussion p.9; no significant pairwise differences after Holm correction, Results 3.2). So CMJ_mean is NOT well supported as this study's primary outcome. (2) Separately and confusingly, the word 'primary' IS used explicitly in Methods, but only for a distinct set of ACUTE within-session fatigue outcomes: 'LMMs were fitted for each primary fatigue-related outcome (MPV, VL, changes in CMJ and RSI mod.)...' (Section 2.4.3, p.4). This 'CMJ' is the acute pre-to-post-set jump-height CHANGE recorded after each of the 12 training sessions (Fatigue sheet: CMJ_pre_mean/CMJ_post_mean per session), a conceptually different variable from the chronic pre-intervention-vs-post-intervention CMJ height (Table 2 / Tests sheet) that outcome_var=CMJ_mean/time_var=Time/primary_time=post in the registry targets. So even the label 'CMJ' is ambiguous between two different constructs in this paper. (3) Methodologically, even restricting to the intended chronic CMJ height: the authors' deposited R code ('Analyses Chronic.R') shows the actually PUBLISHED CMJ model was fitted on the 'Performance' sheet using ALL 14 assessment occasions (pre-intervention + 12 weekly in-training CMJ recordings + post-intervention) with an AR(1) correlation structure and CMJ baseline as an added covariate (group x time interaction chi2(13) = 32.40, p = 0.002) -- NOT a simple two-timepoint pre/post model. The registry's 'Langformat pre/post' description and the two-row-per-participant 'Tests' sheet (ID, Group, Sex, Time=pre/post, CMJ_mean) reproduce Table 2's descriptive means but do NOT reproduce the model/inferential statistic the paper actually reports for chronic CMJ; a faithful reanalysis of chronic CMJ would need the 14-timepoint 'Performance' sheet, AR(1) structure and baseline covariate, not just sheet 'Tests'. (4) control_arm_matches='yes': TS (traditional/continuous-set training) is consistently treated as the comparator/standard method versus CS (cluster-set training) as the experimental intervention, consistent with registry's arm_control=TS. (5) covars_published='Age,Sex' in the registry only half matches: only Sex is used as a covariate in any published model; Age is never a model covariate (only an eligibility/descriptive variable).

analysis_method_quote: 2.4.2 Modelling Approach: 'LMMs were employed to account for repeated measures and interindividual variability. Unless otherwise specified, all models included fixed effects for group, session (acute effects) or time (chronic effects, including pre- and posttests), their interaction, and sex as a covariate with random intercepts for participants to account for individual differences... Statistical significance of fixed effects was assessed using Type III ANOVA with Satterthwaite's method (Satterthwaite 1946). Where significant interactions or main effects were found, post hoc comparisons of estimated marginal means (EMMs) were conducted and adjusted for multiple comparisons via Holm's method (Holm 1979).' (p.4). 2.4.4 Chronic Adaptations: 'To assess chronic training adaptations, LMMs were fitted for 1RM, relative isometric peak force, CMJ, v70 and muscular endurance (maximum repetitions). Baseline values for each respective outcome were initially included as covariates in all models to assess baseline-adjusted change. For CMJ and v70, this baseline-adjusted model was retained as it improved model fit and appropriately accounted for a baseline difference in v70. Conversely, for 1RM, isometric peak force and muscular endurance, the baseline covariate was removed, as its inclusion did not improve model fit and, in some cases, worsened residual diagnostics.' (p.4-5). Section 2.1 Participants (sample-size justification): 'An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power... to estimate the required sample size to detect a medium effect size (f = 0.25) for changes in one-repetition maximum (1RM) in a repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) with two groups and two time points (pre- and post-intervention)... the analysis indicated a required total sample size of 34 participants.' (p.2).
notes: This is a strength-training (exercise-physiology) study, not a clinical/patient trial. The paper has NO single declared primary outcome; it is explicitly dual-focus ('Acute Responses AND Chronic Adaptations'), with many outcomes reported in each domain and no formal trial registration (only an OSF repository for data/code, not pre-registration). Candidates considered for 'first-named/primary' outcome, in descending order of textual support: (a) 1RM (chosen here) -- supported by the a-priori power calculation explicitly built around 1RM change and by being first-named among chronic outcomes in abstract/Methods/Results; (b) the acute 'primary fatigue-related outcome' quartet explicitly labelled 'primary' in Methods 2.4.3 (MPV, VL, acute CMJ-height change, RSI-mod change), first-named MPV -- but this is the ACUTE, within-session domain, not the post-intervention chronic domain the registry's primary_time='post' implies; (c) the literal first specific outcome named anywhere in the abstract, which is blood lactate (within the list of acute objective measures); (d) CMJ height chronic (the registry's chosen outcome) -- weakest candidate: 4th of 5 chronic outcomes named, explicitly non-significant/null result, and its published statistical model used 14 timepoints with AR(1) + baseline covariate rather than a simple 2-timepoint comparison. Sample: two recruitment waves (Oct-Dec 2024, Apr-Jun 2025); randomisation stratified/matched by sex and relative 1RM strength, but only Sex is retained as a model covariate for 1RM (the 1RM/strength matching factor itself was tested as a covariate for CMJ/v70 only, and even there only for those two outcomes). No dropouts are described (36 randomised = 36 analysed = 19 CS + 17 TS). Open access article (European Journal of Sport Science, Wiley-VCH on behalf of ECSS); funding: 'The authors have nothing to report' (Open Access funding via Projekt DEAL); no conflicts of interest declared; ethics approval EKS V 2024_18 (Ruhr University Bochum).
